7	
8	# PRD: Tidewatch
9	*Working title — confirm.*
10	
11	## 0. Document Purpose
12	
13	This PRD specifies Tidewatch, an offline-first field inspection app for municipal water-main inspectors, for the product manager, pilot-city stakeholders (utility IT/security, GIS/asset management, compliance, field operations), and downstream workflow owners (UX, architecture, epic/story breakdown). It is structured so that Glossary terms (§3) are used verbatim throughout, user journeys (§2.3) are referenced by ID from the functional requirements that realize them (§4), and every `[ASSUMPTION]` made in the absence of confirmed input is both tagged inline and indexed in §9 for explicit sign-off. No prior inputs (brief, research, UX docs) existed for this PRD; it was built from a single founding brain-dump plus targeted web research on comparable products, offline-sync patterns, and the regulatory landscape — all folded in below rather than kept as a separate document.
14	
15	## 1. Vision
16	
17	Municipal water utilities run safety- and compliance-critical field programs — exercising every valve on a schedule so it doesn't seize before an emergency, flow-testing hydrants so fire response has the pressure it needs, verifying backflow preventers so contaminated water can't siphon into the drinking supply — on paper checklists and a pocket camera. The paper doesn't argue back: GPS coordinates get typed from memory and are wrong, photos get separated from the finding they were evidence for, and a finding sits in a clipboard for days before it becomes a work order. When a state auditor asks for the trail, someone reconstructs it from scanned PDFs. When a valve-exercise program falls behind cadence, nobody notices until the valve fails during a main break.
18	
19	Tidewatch replaces that paper trail with a field app built for the conditions it will actually be used in — gloved hands, sun glare, concrete vaults with no signal — and a companion web app for the people who schedule the work, review exceptions, and answer to regulators. It captures inspections offline for days at a time, ties every finding to a GPS-verified, auditor's-identity-and-equipment-stamped, photo- and signature-backed record the moment it's created, and syncs it the instant a connection appears — without losing data when two field crews touch the same asset while both were offline. It writes clean corrections back to the utility's GIS asset register instead of letting field reality and the official record drift apart, and it turns four days of paper re-keying into a work order that exists within the same shift the problem was found.
20	
21	For a mid-size utility piloting Tidewatch, success looks like this: the valve-exercising program runs entirely through the app, with nobody keeping a parallel paper trail "just in case," and the 4-day gap between an inspector finding something wrong and a work order existing to fix it collapses to under four hours — without inspectors spending any longer per inspection than they did with a clipboard.
22	
23	## 2. Target User
24	
25	### 2.1 Jobs To Be Done
26	
27	- **Field inspectors** — capture an accurate, defensible finding on the first try, even with no signal and gloves on, without having to re-key or reconcile it later; protect themselves from "did you actually test this" disputes with a timestamped, located, photographed record.
28	- **Dispatchers/supervisors** — know where every crew and every overdue asset stands without waiting for end-of-day paper to land on a desk; spend review time only on findings that are actually anomalous, not re-reading everything that went fine.
29	- **Compliance auditors** — produce a regulator-ready packet for a reporting period without manually reconstructing history from scanned PDFs and whoever remembers what happened.
30	- **GIS analysts** — keep the asset register accurate as field reality changes (a relocated valve, a replaced hydrant) without manual re-entry from field notes, and without untrusted field edits landing directly in the system of record.
31	- **Contractors** (secondary) — get exactly the access needed for a time-boxed engagement, nothing more, without becoming a standing account someone has to remember to deactivate.
32	
33	### 2.2 Non-Users (v1)
34	
35	- Residents/customers receiving outage notifications — no customer-facing surface in v1.
36	- Hydraulic modeling engineers — modeling is out of scope.
37	- Meter-reading/AMI field staff — different workflow, different asset class, out of scope.
38	- Sewer and stormwater field crews — v1 is water mains only.
39	- Drone/robotic-crawler operators — parked as a future input source, not a v1 user.
40	
41	### 2.3 Key User Journeys
42	
43	- **UJ-1. Marcus exercises a valve in a vault with no signal.**
44	  - **Persona + context:** Marcus, a distribution-system inspector three years in, is working a route of six due valves, two of them in below-grade vaults where his phone shows no bars.
45	  - **Entry state:** Authenticated via SSO earlier that morning while still in range; the day's route was pre-synced to his device before he left the yard.
46	  - **Path:** He scans the valve's NFC tag with his tablet; the asset record resolves instantly from the on-device cache. GPS inside the vault reports a 40-meter accuracy radius — too loose to trust — so instead of typing coordinates from memory, he taps "snap to asset" to anchor the record to the valve's registered location. He opens the Valve Exercise template, enters turn count and torque reading (gloves on, large touch targets, high-contrast mode active against the vault's work light), and the torque reading comes back outside the configured tolerance.
47	  - **Climax:** The template flags the out-of-tolerance reading in-app before submission — he isn't left wondering whether it was fine — and requires a confirming photo of the valve's condition, which he captures; it's compressed on-device and queued with the finding, GPS/timestamp/device metadata intact.
48	  - **Resolution:** The finding sits queued, marked clearly as "not yet synced," and surfaces in Dana's exception queue (UJ-2) the moment his tablet finds signal back at the truck.
49	  - **Edge case:** If another inspector had already logged turn-count data on the same valve earlier that day while both were offline, the two edits merge field-by-field on sync; only if they'd both changed the *same* field does it route to a manual-merge review instead of auto-resolving.
50	
51	- **UJ-2. Dana plans routes in the morning and clears exceptions in the afternoon.**
52	  - **Persona + context:** Dana is a field-operations supervisor managing 14 inspectors across a district.
53	  - **Entry state:** Logged into the supervisor web app at her desk, start of shift.
54	  - **Path:** She generates the day's routes; the planner batches nearby due/overdue assets per crew, already filtering out any asset a crew isn't certified or truck-equipped for (a backflow test doesn't land on a crew without a tester). She adjusts one assignment by hand when she knows a crew is running behind. Mid-afternoon, Marcus's out-of-tolerance torque reading (UJ-1) lands in her review queue alongside two other flagged findings — the 40 inspections that came back clean never show up here at all.
55	  - **Climax:** She reviews the flagged torque reading and photo, confirms it's a real problem, and escalates it directly to a work order — no re-typing the finding into a separate system.
56	  - **Resolution:** The work order exists in the utility's work-order system within minutes of her decision, roughly four hours after Marcus logged the finding, not four days.
57	  - **Edge case:** If the work-order system's API is briefly unreachable, the escalation queues and retries automatically; she sees its status as "pending" rather than losing track of whether it went through.
58	
59	- **UJ-3. Renée assembles the quarterly regulatory packet.**
60	  - **Persona + context:** Renée is the utility's compliance auditor, responsible for the state primacy agency's backflow-prevention reporting.
61	  - **Entry state:** Logged into the web app, end of the reporting quarter.
62	  - **Path:** She selects the reporting period and the backflow-preventer-test inspection type; the system compiles every finding in scope.
63	  - **Climax:** The generated packet (PDF narrative + CSV data) lists, per finding: inspector identity, timestamp, GPS-verified location, equipment used (tester make/model and calibration date), the raw reading and pass/fail determination, and the attached photo — exactly what the state expects to see, with nothing reconstructed from memory.
64	  - **Resolution:** She submits the packet to the state agency and files it; if it's ever challenged, the underlying immutable audit log stands behind every number in it.
65	  - **Edge case:** One finding was corrected after initial submission (a mistyped reading); the packet reflects the corrected value, and the audit log shows both the original entry and the correction with its reason code — not a silent overwrite.
66	
67	- **UJ-4. Oscar reconciles a field-discovered asset change.**
68	  - **Persona + context:** Oscar is the utility's GIS analyst, owner of the authoritative asset register.
69	  - **Entry state:** Logged into the web app; a notification shows a pending asset-register write-back awaiting his review.
70	  - **Path:** An inspection recorded a hydrant roughly 12 meters from its registered location — likely relocated during an earlier main repair and never updated in GIS. Oscar reviews the proposed correction against the live feature service, checks the supporting photo and GPS accuracy radius, and approves the write-back rather than letting it commit automatically.
71	  - **Climax:** The asset register updates, and the correction carries the same per-field provenance (who proposed it, who approved it, when) as any other change — the register stays trustworthy specifically because field edits don't bypass his review.
72	  - **Resolution:** He also clears a stuck work-order sync retry he noticed on the same screen, confirming it's now delivered.
73	
74	- **UJ-5. A contractor technician runs backflow tests on a time-boxed account.** *(lighter)* A contracted backflow-test technician is provisioned an account scoped to three districts and the Backflow-Preventer Test template only, set to expire automatically at the end of the 60-day engagement; she captures findings the same way an employee inspector would, but can't see routes, templates, or districts outside her scope, and loses access the moment the engagement window closes without anyone having to remember to deactivate her.

76	## 3. Glossary
77	
78	- **Asset** — A piece of water-main infrastructure Tidewatch tracks (valve, hydrant, backflow-preventer device, or main segment). Has a registered location in the Asset Register.
79	- **Asset Register** — The utility's authoritative GIS system of record for assets (an Esri-compatible feature service), external to Tidewatch. Tidewatch reads from it and proposes write-backs; it does not replace it.
80	- **Inspection Template** — A configurable definition of an inspection type's fields, required evidence, and pass/fail tolerances. V1 ships four: Hydrant Flow Test, Valve Exercise, Main-Break Triage, Backflow-Preventer Test.
81	- **Finding** — A single completed (or in-progress) inspection record produced from an Inspection Template against one Asset.
82	- **Exception** — A Finding that is out-of-tolerance per its template's configured thresholds, or carries an unresolved sync Conflict; the only kind of Finding that enters a supervisor's Review Queue.
83	- **District** — A geographic/organizational grouping of Assets used for route planning, access scoping, and cadence-compliance reporting.
84	- **Route** — A batched set of due/overdue Assets assigned to a Crew for a given day.
85	- **Crew** — One or more field inspectors assigned to a Route, with associated skill certifications and truck equipment.
86	- **Reporting Period** — A date range (e.g., a quarter) used to scope a Regulatory Packet or cadence-compliance view.
87	- **Regulatory Packet** — An exported PDF narrative + CSV data bundle of Findings scoped to a Reporting Period and inspection type, built for submission to a regulator or for internal asset-management reporting.
88	- **Immutable Audit Log** — The append-only record of every create/edit/approve/export action in the system; corrections append new entries with reason codes and never overwrite prior values.
89	- **Provenance** — Per-field metadata (last-editor user ID, device ID, timestamp) retained for every field on every record, feeding both Conflict detection and the Immutable Audit Log.
90	- **Conflict** — A sync-time state where the same field on the same record was changed by two users since their last common sync point; routed to manual merge rather than auto-resolved.
91	- **Sync Cycle** — The process by which a device's queued offline changes are reconciled with the backend, field by field, when connectivity is available.
92	- **Snap-to-Asset** — A one-tap correction that anchors a Finding's location to an Asset's registered location when captured GPS falls within a configured tolerance of it, replacing manual coordinate entry.
93	- **Accuracy Radius** — The reported confidence radius of a GPS fix at time of capture, recorded alongside the coordinates.
94	- **Turn Count / Torque** — Valve Exercise template fields recording how many turns were applied to operate a valve and the torque measured while doing so.
95	- **Cadence Compliance** — The percentage of Assets of a given type inspected within their required/recommended schedule (e.g., valves exercised on time), reportable by District.
96	- **Device-Bound Token** — An authentication token tied to one registered device; revocable independently of the user's account.
97	- **Contractor Account** — A Role-scoped account with a configured expiration date/time and restricted District/Template access, for non-employee field staff.
98	- **Work Order** — A task record in the utility's external work-order system, created from an escalated Finding.
99	
100	## 4. Features
101	
102	### 4.1 Offline-First Sync & Data Integrity
103	
104	**Description:** The foundation the rest of the product depends on: the field app must be fully usable for days with no connectivity, and when connectivity returns, queued changes must reconcile without silently losing an edit or silently overwriting someone else's. Conflict resolution and per-field provenance are specified together because they share one mechanism — a per-field last-writer record is both how a conflict gets detected and how the audit log answers "who touched this." Realizes UJ-1, UJ-4.
105	
106	**Functional Requirements:**
107	
108	#### FR-1: Extended offline operation
109	A field inspector can create, edit, and complete Findings — including photo and signature capture — entirely offline for at least 5 consecutive days.
110	**Consequences (testable):**
111	- All four v1 Inspection Templates remain fully fillable with zero network calls required to complete and locally save a Finding.
112	- A device with no connectivity for 5 full days shows no data loss or forced-login interruption blocking continued inspection work.
113	
114	#### FR-2: Per-field provenance
115	Every field value on every record carries the identity of the user and device that last wrote it, and the timestamp of that write, retained as history rather than overwritten.
116	**Consequences (testable):**
117	- Any field's current value can be traced to a specific (user, device, timestamp) triple via the audit view (FR-23).
118	- Overwriting a field's value does not delete the prior (user, device, timestamp, value) entry — it is retained as history.
119	
120	#### FR-3: Deterministic conflict resolution
121	At Sync Cycle time, the system compares each field's BASE (last commonly-synced value), YOURS (local edit), and THEIRS (current server value); fields changed on only one side merge automatically, and only fields changed on both sides since BASE are flagged as a Conflict for manual resolution.
122	**Consequences (testable):**
123	- Two offline edits to different fields of the same record both survive a sync with no manual intervention.
124	- Two offline edits to the *same* field of the same record by different users produce exactly one Conflict entry, never a silent overwrite of either value.
125	- Fields marked as derived/calculated in a template are excluded from field-level auto-merge and always route to manual review if touched on both sides. `[ASSUMPTION: no derived/calculated fields are defined in the four v1 templates, so this exclusion has no immediate effect but is specified to avoid silent corruption if templates gain calculated fields later.]`
126	- Photo and signature attachment fields use additive-union merge (multiple photos attached by different offline users to the same Finding are all retained) rather than scalar BASE/YOURS/THEIRS comparison; a single-valued attachment slot (e.g., the one required signature) edited on both sides since BASE produces a Conflict, the same as a scalar field. `[ASSUMPTION: attachment fields need a merge rule distinct from scalar fields, since "both sides changed the same field" doesn't map cleanly onto a photo array — specified now rather than left implicit.]`
127	
128	#### FR-4: Sync performance
129	A full day's queued data for one device — up to 200 Findings with attached photos — completes syncing within 90 seconds against the reference weak-LTE profile defined in §6 Cross-Cutting NFRs.
130	**Consequences (testable):**
131	- Photos are compressed on-device (FR-14) and queued before sync begins, not compressed during sync.
132	- Sync transmits only changed fields/attachments per record (delta sync), not a full-record re-upload, to meet the 90-second target. `[ASSUMPTION: delta/field-level sync is necessary to hit this target per offline-sync research; full-record sync was found in comparable products to be the usual bottleneck.]`
133	
134	#### FR-5: Sync status visibility
135	Field and supervisor UIs display per-record sync state (queued, syncing, synced, conflict) at all times.
136	**Consequences (testable):**
137	- An inspector can distinguish a locally-saved-but-unsynced Finding from a confirmed-synced one without leaving the Finding list view.
138	- A Finding in "conflict" state is visually distinguishable from "queued" and cannot be mistaken for successfully submitted.
139	
140	### 4.2 Asset Identification & Lookup
141	
142	**Description:** Inspectors must be able to identify the correct Asset without typing anything from memory, under three different field conditions: a readable tag, no tag but a map, or neither. Realizes UJ-1.
143	
144	**Functional Requirements:**
145	
146	#### FR-6: Scan-based lookup
147	An inspector can identify an Asset by scanning its QR code or NFC tag, resolving to the cached Asset record even with no connectivity.
148	**Consequences (testable):**
149	- Scanning a tag for an Asset pre-synced to the device resolves to the correct Asset record in under 2 seconds with no network call.
150	- Scanning an unrecognized or damaged tag surfaces a clear fallback prompt to map-based or nearest-N lookup rather than a dead end.
151	
152	#### FR-7: Map-based lookup (offline-capable)
153	An inspector can locate and select an Asset from a map view showing cached Asset positions and basemap tiles, without connectivity. `[ASSUMPTION: offline *viewing* of pre-synced maps/asset layers is in scope for v1 — only offline map *authoring* was named out of scope by the user; basemap tiles and Asset layers for an inspector's assigned Routes/District are pre-synced whenever the device has connectivity.]`
154	**Consequences (testable):**
155	- With no connectivity, an inspector can open the map view and see Asset pins for every Asset on their currently assigned Route.
156	- Selecting a pin opens the same Asset record FR-6 would have resolved to.
157	
158	#### FR-8: Nearest-N lookup
159	An inspector can request the N nearest Assets (N configurable per deployment) to their current GPS position when scan and map identification aren't viable (e.g., missing/damaged tag, position not on today's Route).
160	**Consequences (testable):**
161	- The nearest-N list returns Assets sorted by distance from current position, resolvable even with degraded GPS accuracy (using best-available fix).
162	- Selecting an Asset from the list opens the same Asset record as FR-6/FR-7.
163	
164	#### FR-9: GPS capture with accuracy radius
165	Every location-bearing record captures GPS coordinates and the device-reported accuracy radius at time of capture.
166	**Consequences (testable):**
167	- Every Finding stores a coordinate pair and a numeric accuracy-radius value, both visible in the audit view.
168	- GPS is captured on-demand at the moment of Asset identification/Finding creation, not via continuous background tracking. `[ASSUMPTION: fix-on-capture rather than continuous tracking, to meet the <15%/8hr battery NFR per research — continuous high-accuracy GPS was flagged as a major, avoidable drain.]`
169	- If no GPS fix is obtainable at all — common in below-grade concrete vaults, and distinct from a low-accuracy fix — the Finding is still completable with location explicitly flagged "no fix" rather than blocked or silently stored as a stale/zero coordinate; it queues for manual location reconciliation (e.g., a supervisor assigns the Asset's registered location) rather than being treated as accurate data.
170	
171	#### FR-10: Snap-to-asset correction
172	When captured GPS falls within a configured tolerance of a known Asset's registered location, the system offers a one-tap correction anchoring the Finding to that Asset's registered coordinates instead of the raw GPS fix.
173	**Consequences (testable):**
174	- Within tolerance, "snap to asset" is offered as a single tap and, once accepted, the Finding's recorded location is the Asset's registered coordinate, with the raw GPS fix and accuracy radius retained alongside it for audit purposes (not discarded).
175	- No free-text manual coordinate entry is offered as an alternative path, in either in- or out-of-tolerance cases. `[ASSUMPTION: removing manual coordinate typing entirely, rather than offering it as a fallback, best serves the stated goal of eliminating "typed from memory" GPS errors — out-of-tolerance cases fall back to the raw captured fix (or to the "no fix" flag of FR-9, when there is no fix at all), not manual entry.]`
176	
177	### 4.3 Inspection Templates & Evidence Capture
178	
179	**Description:** The actual inspection workflows inspectors run, and the evidence discipline that makes a Finding defensible later. Realizes UJ-1.
180	
181	**Functional Requirements:**
182	
183	#### FR-11: Configurable inspection templates
184	An administrator can configure an Inspection Template's fields, required evidence, and pass/fail tolerances without code changes. V1 ships four built-in templates: Hydrant Flow Test, Valve Exercise, Main-Break Triage, Backflow-Preventer Test.
185	**Consequences (testable):**
186	- All four v1 templates are usable out of the box with no configuration required before first use.
187	- An administrator can add, remove, or re-tolerance a field on an existing template through the web app without a code deployment.
188	
189	#### FR-12: Valve exercise fields
190	The Valve Exercise template captures Turn Count and Torque readings and evaluates them against Asset-specific expected ranges.
191	**Consequences (testable):**
192	- Submitting a Torque reading outside the configured tolerance for that Asset marks the Finding an Exception (FR-20) before submission completes.
193	- Turn Count and Torque are both individually retained with Provenance (FR-2), not collapsed into a single pass/fail flag.
194	
195	#### FR-13: Required photo evidence
196	A template can mark photo capture as required; submission is blocked until the required photo(s) are attached.
197	**Consequences (testable):**
198	- Attempting to submit a Finding missing a template-required photo is blocked with a clear in-app message identifying what's missing.
199	- Once attached, the required photo cannot be submitted without its embedded EXIF metadata intact (FR-14).
200	
201	#### FR-14: On-device photo compression
202	Captured photos (up to 12MP source resolution) are compressed on-device before being queued for sync, while preserving embedded EXIF (GPS, timestamp, device) for chain-of-custody.
203	**Consequences (testable):**
204	- A 12MP source photo is reduced to a long-edge resolution and JPEG quality that preserves visual evidentiary quality while materially reducing sync payload size. `[ASSUMPTION: target ~2000-3000px long edge at ~70-85% JPEG quality, per industry-convergent practice found in research — no utility-specific evidentiary standard was identified, so this is a starting point subject to pilot validation.]`
205	- Compression happens exactly once, at capture time; a photo is never recompressed on subsequent sync retries or handling, consistent with chain-of-custody practice.
206	
207	#### FR-15: Signature capture
208	A template can require an on-screen signature (inspector, and optionally a witness or property owner) attached to the Finding.
209	**Consequences (testable):**
210	- A template configured to require a signature blocks submission until it's captured, the same way FR-13 blocks on a missing required photo.
211	- The captured signature is stored as part of the immutable Finding record with the same Provenance treatment as any other field.
212	
213	#### FR-16: Accessibility of field capture
214	The field UI supports large touch targets and a high-contrast display mode suitable for gloved hands and direct sunlight.
215	**Consequences (testable):**
216	- All primary actions (template field entry, photo capture, signature, submit) meet a minimum touch target of 9mm (approximately 44x44px at standard device density). `[ASSUMPTION: 9mm/44px follows common platform HIG convention for glove-compatible targets; validate against pilot usability testing with actual field gloves.]`
217	- High-contrast mode is toggleable and provides a minimum contrast ratio of 7:1 between foreground and background, exceeding WCAG 2.2 AA's 4.5:1 floor given the outdoor-glare use case. `[ASSUMPTION: 7:1 is a starting target, not a utility-confirmed requirement.]`
218	
219	### 4.4 Route Planning & Dispatch
220	
221	**Description:** How dispatchers turn a list of due/overdue Assets into assignable work for specific crews. Realizes UJ-2.
222	
223	**Functional Requirements:**
224	
225	#### FR-17: Batch route planning
226	A dispatcher/supervisor can generate a Route that batches nearby due/overdue Assets for a given Crew and date.
227	**Consequences (testable):**
228	- Generating a Route for a Crew/date returns a set of geographically clustered due/overdue Assets rather than an unordered list.
229	- A generated Route is editable before being published to the Crew's devices.
230	
231	#### FR-18: Crew/equipment matching
232	The route planner excludes Assets a Crew isn't certified for or a Crew's truck isn't equipped to inspect (e.g., a Backflow-Preventer Test isn't assigned to a Crew without a certified tester and the right equipment).
233	**Consequences (testable):**
234	- A Crew lacking a configured certification never receives an Asset requiring that certification in a generated Route.
235	- Overriding this exclusion requires an explicit manual reassignment (FR-19), not a silent planner bypass.
236	
237	#### FR-19: Route reassignment
238	A dispatcher can manually reassign an Asset from one Route/Crew to another before or during the day.
239	**Consequences (testable):**
240	- Reassigning an Asset removes it from the original Crew's device view and adds it to the new Crew's, reflected on next sync.
241	- A reassignment is itself an audited action (FR-23), attributable to the dispatcher who made it.
242	
243	### 4.5 Supervisor Review & Exception Triage
244	
245	**Description:** The review workflow that lets a supervisor cover far more ground than reading every Finding — only Exceptions reach them. Realizes UJ-2.
246	
247	**Functional Requirements:**
248	
249	#### FR-20: Exception-based review queue
250	The supervisor Review Queue surfaces only Findings that are out-of-tolerance per their Template's configured thresholds, or carry an unresolved Conflict — not every submitted Finding.
251	**Consequences (testable):**
252	- A Finding within tolerance and with no Conflict never appears in the Review Queue.
253	- An out-of-tolerance Finding or a Conflicted Finding always appears, with the reason it was flagged visible at a glance.
254	
255	#### FR-21: Finding disposition
256	A supervisor can approve, reject-with-reason, or escalate-to-work-order a flagged Finding.
257	**Consequences (testable):**
258	- Each disposition action is recorded against the Finding with the supervisor's identity and timestamp (feeding FR-23).
259	- "Reject" requires a reason to be entered before the action completes.
260	
261	#### FR-22: Exception notifications
262	Supervisors receive an in-app and email notification when a new Exception enters their Review Queue. `[ASSUMPTION: in-app + email covers v1; SMS/push-to-phone for time-sensitive exceptions (e.g., a failed backflow test) is deferred pending confirmation of how time-sensitive these actually need to be — see §8 Open Questions.]`
263	**Consequences (testable):**
264	- A new Exception triggers exactly one email and one in-app notification to the Finding's assigned supervisor, not a notification per minor field within it.
265	- Notification delivery failure (e.g., bad email address) is logged and surfaced to an administrator rather than silently dropped.
266	
267	### 4.6 Audit Trail & Regulatory Reporting
268	
269	**Description:** What makes a Finding usable as evidence months or years later, and how that evidence gets bundled for a regulator. Realizes UJ-3.
270	
271	**Functional Requirements:**
272	
273	#### FR-23: Immutable audit log
274	Every create/edit/approve/export action across Findings, Assets, and Work Orders is appended to an immutable, append-only audit log; corrections are recorded as new entries with reason codes, never overwriting prior values.
275	**Consequences (testable):**
276	- Editing a previously-submitted Finding's field produces a new audit-log entry with a reason code, while the prior entry remains readable, not deleted.
277	- The audit log cannot be edited or deleted through any application-level action available to any role, including administrator.
278	
279	#### FR-24: Regulatory packet export
280	An auditor can generate a Regulatory Packet (PDF narrative + CSV data) scoped to a Reporting Period and Inspection Template type.
281	**Consequences (testable):**
282	- Selecting a Reporting Period and Template type produces a PDF and a CSV covering exactly the Findings of that type completed within that period.
283	- The export completes and is downloadable without requiring any manual data assembly outside the app.
284	
285	#### FR-25: Evidence bundling in export
286	The Regulatory Packet includes, per Finding: inspector identity, timestamp, GPS-verified location, equipment used (including calibration date where applicable), raw readings and pass/fail determination, and attached photos.
287	**Consequences (testable):**
288	- Every Finding in an exported packet shows all six evidence elements with no "data not available" gaps for Findings captured through the app.
289	- Equipment calibration date is present for any Template field that designates calibrated-equipment evidence (e.g., torque wrench, flow gauge). `[ASSUMPTION: equipment/calibration metadata is entered or selected by the inspector at capture time from a utility-maintained equipment register — the mechanism for maintaining that register is not yet specified; see §8 Open Questions.]`
290	
291	#### FR-26: Audit log and record retention
292	The audit log and underlying records are retained per a utility-configurable retention policy.
293	**Consequences (testable):**
294	- A utility can configure a retention period at or above a 7-year default floor. `[ASSUMPTION: 7-year default, informed by typical multi-year audit/asset-management cycles found in research (AWWA/GASB-adjacent practice); no single confirmed statutory number applies across states — treat as a starting default pending each pilot city's actual requirement.]`
295	- No record subject to an active retention policy can be purged, by any role, before its retention period elapses.
296	
297	### 4.7 Asset Register & Work-Order Integration
298	
299	**Description:** How Tidewatch stays a field layer on top of each utility's existing systems of record rather than becoming a second, competing one. Realizes UJ-4, UJ-2.
300	
301	**Functional Requirements:**
302	
303	#### FR-27: Two-way asset register sync
304	The system synchronizes Asset records bidirectionally with the utility's GIS feature service (Esri-compatible); field-discovered corrections write back only after GIS analyst review and approval.
305	**Consequences (testable):**
306	- A field-discovered Asset-location discrepancy generates a pending write-back proposal visible to a GIS analyst, not an automatic commit to the feature service.
307	- Approving a proposal commits the change to the feature service and records the approver via Provenance; rejecting it discards the proposed change without touching the register.
308	- A new proposal for an Asset that already has a pending proposal updates that existing proposal rather than creating a second parallel one, so repeated field revisits of the same discrepancy don't pile up redundant approval items.
309	- `[ASSUMPTION: approval-gated write-back, rather than auto-commit, given the Asset Register is explicitly the utility's system of record and research found existing GIS-native tools treat it the same way (versioned-geodatabase reconcile workflows).]`
310	
311	#### FR-28: Work-order creation
312	An escalated Finding (FR-21) can generate a Work Order via a generic REST adapter to the utility's work-order system, or via CSV export/import when no API integration exists.
313	**Consequences (testable):**
314	- Escalating a Finding with an active REST integration configured creates a corresponding Work Order in the external system within the integration's normal latency, without manual re-entry.
315	- With no REST integration configured, the same escalation produces a CSV row in a scheduled/on-demand export containing the same Finding data.
316	
317	#### FR-29: Integration failure handling
318	If an Asset-register or work-order integration endpoint is unreachable, pending sync operations queue and retry, surfaced via a status view rather than silently dropping.
319	**Consequences (testable):**
320	- A failed write-back or work-order creation attempt is retried automatically and shows as "pending/retrying" in a status view visible to a GIS analyst or administrator.
321	- No pending integration operation is ever silently discarded; every failure path ends in either success or a visible, actionable "failed" state.
322	- Retries use exponential backoff and stop automatically after a maximum attempt count `[ASSUMPTION: retrying over a 24-hour window]`, after which the operation moves to a "failed — needs attention" state requiring explicit administrator/analyst action rather than retrying indefinitely.
323	
324	### 4.8 Identity, Access & Contractor Management
325	
326	**Description:** Who gets into the system, what they can do once they're in, and how access ends cleanly when it should. Realizes UJ-5.
327	
328	**Functional Requirements:**
329	
330	#### FR-30: SSO authentication
331	Users authenticate via the utility's identity provider using a standard SSO protocol. `[ASSUMPTION: standards-based SAML/OIDC support is sufficient for v1 rather than bespoke per-IdP integrations — specific pilot-city IdPs (Azure AD, Okta, ADFS, etc.) are unconfirmed; see §8 Open Questions.]`
332	**Consequences (testable):**
333	- A user provisioned in the utility's IdP can authenticate into Tidewatch without a separate Tidewatch-managed password.
334	- Deactivating a user in the utility's IdP revokes their Tidewatch access on next token refresh at the latest.
335	
336	#### FR-31: Role-based access control
337	The system enforces role-scoped permissions for Field Inspector, Supervisor/Dispatcher, Auditor, GIS Analyst, Contractor, and Administrator roles, each restricted to the actions/data their role requires.
338	**Consequences (testable):**
339	- A Field Inspector cannot access the Review Queue, Regulatory Packet export, or Asset Register write-back approval screens.
340	- A Contractor account (FR-33) cannot access roles' screens/data outside its configured District and Template scope, even with a valid session.
341	- Administrator is the only role permitted to edit Inspection Templates (FR-11), trigger remote wipe (FR-32), and provision or expire Contractor accounts (FR-33).
342	
343	#### FR-32: Device-bound tokens & remote wipe
344	Authentication tokens are bound to the registered device; an administrator can remotely revoke a device's access and wipe its locally cached data.
345	**Consequences (testable):**
346	- A token issued to one device cannot be used to authenticate from a different, unregistered device.
347	- Triggering remote wipe on a device clears its locally cached Findings, Asset data, and credentials on next connectivity, and the device can no longer sync until re-registered.
348	- A device-bound token remains usable offline for up to `[ASSUMPTION: 7 days]` without server contact — slightly beyond the 5-day offline floor (FR-1) — after which the device locks out of further local record creation until it reconnects and re-validates; this bounds how long a stolen or deactivated device can stay functional while kept deliberately offline.
349	
350	#### FR-33: Contractor time-boxed accounts
351	An administrator can provision a Contractor account scoped to specific Assets/Districts and Templates, with an expiration date/time after which access is automatically revoked.
352	**Consequences (testable):**
353	- A Contractor account's access ends automatically at its configured expiration, with no administrator action required at expiry time.
354	- A Contractor account can only see/act on the Districts and Templates explicitly configured for it. `[ASSUMPTION: default maximum expiration of 90 days, administrator-configurable shorter or longer per engagement, pending confirmation of typical contractor engagement length.]`
355	
356	### 4.9 Cadence Compliance Analytics
357	
358	**Description:** The view that answers "are we actually keeping up with the valve-exercise program," which today nobody can answer without manually counting paper. Realizes the business goal in §1 Vision directly, rather than a specific UJ.
359	
360	**Functional Requirements:**
361	
362	#### FR-34: Cadence compliance dashboard
363	Supervisors/Dispatchers can view the percentage of Assets of a given type (starting with valves) exercised/tested on schedule, broken out by District.
364	**Consequences (testable):**
365	- The dashboard shows, per District, the percentage of due Assets that were inspected within their required cadence window as of the current date.
366	- Filtering by Asset type (valve, hydrant, backflow-preventer) changes the computed percentage accordingly.
367	
368	#### FR-35: Trend view
369	The dashboard shows cadence-compliance trend over a selectable Reporting Period window (e.g., trailing 12 months).
370	**Consequences (testable):**
371	- Selecting a trailing window (e.g., 12 months) renders a trend of the cadence-compliance percentage over that window, not just a current-day snapshot.
372	- The trend view's underlying data matches what a Regulatory Packet (FR-24) would report for the same period, so the two never visibly disagree.
373	
374	## 5. Non-Goals (Explicit)
375	
376	- Tidewatch is not a hydraulic modeling tool — no network simulation, pressure modeling, or capacity planning.
377	- Tidewatch is not a meter-reading/AMI system — no meter data collection or billing-adjacent functionality.
378	- Tidewatch does not cover sewer or stormwater assets in v1 — water mains only.
379	- Tidewatch is not a customer-facing product — no outage notifications or any resident-visible surface.
380	- Tidewatch does not replace the utility's GIS asset register or work-order system — it is a field layer that writes into them under review, not a competing system of record (see FR-27).
381	- Tidewatch does not support offline map *authoring* (editing basemap tiles or Asset layers from the field) — only offline *viewing* of pre-synced data (FR-7).
382	- Tidewatch does not support voice control in v1.
383	- Tidewatch does not ingest drone or robotic-crawler data in v1 — explicitly parked by the product owner as a future consideration, not a rejected one.
384	
385	## 6. Cross-Cutting NFRs
386	
387	- **Offline duration:** Full field-app functionality (FR-1) sustained for at least 5 consecutive days with zero connectivity.
388	- **Sync performance:** A 200-record day syncs within 90 seconds against a reference weak-LTE profile. `[ASSUMPTION: reference profile of ~1 Mbps downlink / 512 kbps uplink, ~150ms latency, ~1% packet loss — no utility-specific network baseline was provided; this should be validated against real pilot-site cellular conditions before launch.]`
389	- **Battery impact:** Field-app battery consumption stays under 15% of an 8-hour shift's battery budget under typical daily use (fix-on-capture GPS per FR-9, batched rather than continuous sync). `[ASSUMPTION: this target is only achievable with duty-cycled GPS and batched sync as specified — continuous background GPS tracking or continuous sync would likely exceed it, per research into comparable field apps.]`
390	- **Device support:** Rugged Android tablets (`[ASSUMPTION: Android 11+]`) and iPhones (`[ASSUMPTION: iOS 16+]`) for the field app; modern evergreen browsers for the supervisor/auditor/GIS-analyst web app.
391	- **Photo handling:** 12MP source photos compressed on-device per FR-14, EXIF-preserving.
392	- **Accessibility:** Supervisor/auditor/GIS-analyst web app meets WCAG 2.2 AA. Field app meets a 9mm/44px minimum touch target and a 7:1 minimum contrast ratio in high-contrast mode for gloved/high-glare use (FR-16), though WCAG itself targets web content and doesn't directly certify a native field app.
393	- **Localization:** Field app ships with English and Spanish UI and Inspection Template field labels (FR-11) for v1; the supervisor/auditor/GIS-analyst web app is English-only for v1. `[ASSUMPTION: English + Spanish covers pilot-crew needs — confirm against actual pilot-city field-crew demographics (Open Question 3); no other languages are assumed in scope.]`
394	- **Data residency:** All production data resides in-region per the deploying utility's jurisdiction. `[ASSUMPTION: "in-region" means the utility's own state/country, deployment-configurable per pilot city rather than a single fixed region — multi-city, potentially multi-region hosting is implied by selling to utilities in different jurisdictions.]`
395	- **Security:** Encryption at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+); device-bound tokens with a capped offline validity period and remote wipe (FR-32); SSO via the utility's identity provider (FR-30). `[ASSUMPTION: a 90-day key-rotation cadence for at-rest encryption keys — no utility-specific key-management policy has been confirmed.]`
396	- **Observability:** Sync failures, integration failures (FR-29), Asset-register write-back approval-queue backlog (FR-27), and Review Queue backlog growth are logged and alertable to operations staff.
397	- **Availability:** Supervisor/auditor/GIS-analyst web app and sync backend target `[ASSUMPTION: 99.5% uptime, excluding scheduled maintenance]` — field inspection work itself is unaffected by backend downtime since it continues fully offline (FR-1). This is a general-availability target, not an incident-response SLA: a backend outage during active review hours draws directly against SM-1's 4-hour finding-to-work-order budget rather than being separately exempted from it (see R10).
398	
399	## 7. Constraints and Guardrails
400	
401	**Privacy:** Tidewatch collects minimal PII — field-staff identity (tied to employment, not customer data) and occasionally property-adjacent photography incidental to an Asset's location. No customer account, billing, or usage data is collected (consistent with meter-reading/AMI being out of scope).
402	
403	**Safety:** Tidewatch is a data-capture and reporting system; it does not actuate valves, pumps, or any physical control system, so no functional-safety (e.g., IEC 61508-class) requirements apply. `[ASSUMPTION: confirm this framing holds if a future version considers any closed-loop control integration — out of scope for v1 as specified.]`
404	
405	**Cost:** No cost ceiling or pricing model was specified by the product owner; flagged as an Open Question (§8) rather than assumed, since it affects packaging decisions this PRD doesn't own.
406	
407	## 8. Stakeholders and Approvals
408	
409	Given 12-18 month municipal procurement cycles, each pilot city will likely route sign-off through several distinct stakeholders rather than a single buyer:
410	
411	- **Utility IT/Security** — SSO integration (FR-30), device management policy, data residency (§6).
412	- **GIS/Asset Management lead** — Asset Register data-model mapping and write-back approval workflow (FR-27).
413	- **Compliance/Regulatory affairs** — Regulatory Packet content (FR-24/25) sign-off against that state's actual requirements.
414	- **Field Operations director** — the likely procurement sponsor; rollout and training plan (§9) sign-off.
415	- **Union/labor representative**, where field staff are organized — device policy and any location-tracking disclosure requirements. `[ASSUMPTION: this stakeholder is relevant for at least some pilot cities given public-sector field workforces are frequently organized; confirm per city.]`
416	
417	## 9. Rollout and Change Management
418	
419	- Phased pilot in 2 cities rather than a simultaneous broad rollout.
420	- A parallel-run period (paper checklists continue alongside the app) before each city formally retires paper for valve exercising — directly de-risks the primary success metric (SM-1) by not forcing a hard cutover before trust is established.
421	- Train-the-trainer model: a small group of lead inspectors per city trained first, then extending to the full field staff.
422	- Pilot feedback loop feeds back into Inspection Template configuration (FR-11) before any wider rollout beyond the 2 pilot cities.
423	
424	## 10. Data Governance
425	
426	- **Residency:** In-region per §6.
427	- **Retention:** Per utility-configurable policy, 7-year default floor (FR-26).
428	- **Classification:** Operational/Asset data is non-PII by default; field-staff identity is the primary PII category, handled as employment-related data rather than customer data (§7 Privacy).
429	
430	## 11. Compliance and Regulatory
431	
432	This section documents the regulatory/standards context Tidewatch's audit and reporting features (§4.6) are built to satisfy — grounded in research rather than assumption, since getting this wrong undermines the product's core value proposition:
433	
434	- **Valve exercising:** No federal mandate; AWWA Manual M44 and ANSI/AWWA G200 are the industry-standard guidance utilities are generally expected to follow or exceed (typically full-system exercise within 5 years, annual for critical large-diameter valves). Individual states/utilities may set stricter cadences in their own O&M manuals.
435	- **Hydrant flow testing:** AWWA M17 and NFPA 291 govern test methodology and procedure (NFPA 291 also covers hydrant color-coding/marking); neither standard itself sets a retest cadence — AWWA M17 recommends a 10-year full-area retest cycle, and the commonly cited "every 5 years" figure belongs to NFPA 25, a different standard, not NFPA 291. ISO's Public Protection Classification program is the practical commercial driver: full insurance credit requires flow data no older than 5 years, with reduced credit on a decay curve out to 10 years and no credit beyond that.
436	- **Backflow-preventer testing:** The one area with direct state regulatory teeth — most states require annual testing by a certified tester under Safe Drinking Water Act primacy delegation, with recordkeeping requirements that vary by state. Local cross-connection-control ordinances often layer on additional device-registration and reporting obligations.
437	- **Asset-management reporting:** GASB 34's "modified approach" lets utilities skip infrastructure depreciation in financial statements if they maintain a current asset inventory, documented condition assessments via a reproducible method performed at least every 3 years, evidence of a maintained condition level, and estimated annual maintenance cost — plus required supplementary disclosure of actual-versus-estimated preservation spending for each of the past 5 reporting periods. §4.6's audit trail and §4.9's cadence dashboard directly support the condition-assessment and spending-disclosure evidence trail this requires. AWWA G200/G400 series provide the underlying voluntary standards of practice for documentation and record retention.
438	- **Accessibility:** WCAG 2.2 AA for the supervisor/auditor/GIS-analyst web app (§6).
439	
440	`[NOTE FOR PM: none of the above are federal mandates for valve/hydrant programs — they're industry-standard practice plus state-specific rules that vary per pilot city. Confirm each pilot city's actual state-level requirements (especially backflow testing specifics) before finalizing Regulatory Packet content with Compliance.]`
441	
442	## 12. Risk and Mitigations
443	
444	- **R1 — GPS inaccuracy, or complete signal loss, underground undermines Snap-to-Asset and location capture.** Mitigated by always displaying accuracy radius (FR-9), providing an explicit "no fix" flag with a manual-reconciliation path when no GPS signal is obtainable at all (FR-9), and falling back to scan/map/nearest-N identification (§4.2) rather than forcing a low-confidence snap.
445	- **R2 — 12-18 month procurement cycles delay pilot start.** Mitigated by engaging IT/Security and Compliance stakeholders (§8) early, in parallel with commercial negotiation rather than sequentially after it.
446	- **R3 — Conflict-resolution edge cases around derived/calculated fields silently corrupt data.** Mitigated by excluding such fields from field-level auto-merge by design (FR-3), even though no v1 template currently defines one.
447	- **R4 — Crew resistance to replacing a familiar paper workflow.** Mitigated by the parallel-run rollout approach (§9) rather than a forced cutover.
448	- **R5 — GIS/work-order system variability across utilities** (Cityworks vs. Lucity vs. none, different Esri configurations). Mitigated by keeping both integrations (FR-27, FR-28) config-driven and generic rather than hard-coded to one vendor, with CSV fallback for utilities with no API-integrated work-order system.
449	- **R6 — State-specific regulatory variance** (especially backflow-testing cadence/recordkeeping). Mitigated by configurable Templates (FR-11) and retention policy (FR-26) rather than one hard-coded ruleset; see §11 note.
450	- **R7 — Battery and sync-performance NFR targets prove infeasible under real field conditions.** Mitigated by validating fix-on-capture GPS and batched/delta sync (§6) against real pilot-site network and device conditions early in the pilot, before wider rollout.
451	- **R8 — Exception-based review queue (FR-20) either misses real problems (tolerances too loose) or buries supervisors (tolerances too tight).** Mitigated by making tolerances configurable per Template (FR-11) and tracked directly via the SM-C2 counter-metric (§13).
452	- **R9 — A stolen or deactivated device kept fully offline indefinitely could retain cached data access, since remote wipe and token revocation (FR-32) both implicitly require connectivity to take effect.** Mitigated by a capped offline token validity period (FR-32) beyond which the device locks out of further local use pending reconnection and re-validation.
453	- **R10 — Approval and retry queues (FR-27 GIS write-back, FR-29 integration retries) could grow silently unbounded** (a GIS analyst on leave; a long-dead work-order integration), with field crews re-flagging the same discrepancy on every revisit. Mitigated by write-back proposal deduplication (FR-27), backlog visibility via §6 Observability, and bounded retry with escalation to a visible "failed" state after a maximum attempt count (FR-29).
454	
455	## 13. MVP Scope
456	
457	### 13.1 In Scope
458	
459	- Offline-first field app (Android + iOS) covering all four v1 Inspection Templates with photo/signature evidence capture, GPS/Snap-to-Asset, and scan/map/nearest-N Asset lookup.
460	- Deterministic, field-level conflict resolution and per-field provenance across all synced data.
461	- Route planning with crew/equipment matching, and a supervisor exception-based review queue with in-app/email notifications.
462	- Immutable audit log and Regulatory Packet (PDF + CSV) export.
463	- Two-way Asset Register sync (Esri-compatible, analyst-approval-gated) and Work Order creation (REST adapter + CSV fallback).
464	- SSO, RBAC across five roles, device-bound tokens with remote wipe, and time-boxed Contractor accounts.
465	- Cadence-compliance dashboard with district breakdown and trend view.
466	- Pilot rollout in 2 cities with a parallel-run period before paper retirement.
467	
468	### 13.2 Out of Scope for MVP
469	
470	- Customer-facing outage notifications — no customer-facing surface planned at all for this product line currently.
471	- Hydraulic modeling — different product category entirely.
472	- Meter reading/AMI — different asset class and workflow.
473	- Sewer and stormwater assets — deferred to a possible v2; water mains only for v1.
474	- Voice control.
475	- Offline map authoring (editing basemap/Asset layers from the field) — offline *viewing* is in scope (FR-7).
476	- Drone/robotic-crawler input sources. `[NOTE FOR PM: explicitly parked, not rejected — the product owner wants this revisited once core v1 is proven; worth a deliberate v2 scoping conversation rather than letting it default away.]`
477	- SMS notifications for exceptions — deferred pending confirmation of how time-sensitive exceptions really need to be (§8 Open Questions).
478	- Pricing/packaging model — a go-to-market concern this PRD doesn't own.
479	
480	## 14. Success Metrics
481	
482	**Primary**
483	- **SM-1:** Finding-to-work-order latency — median elapsed time from Finding submission (FR-13/FR-15 complete) to Work Order creation (FR-28), target under 4 hours in pilot cities, against a stated paper-process baseline of ~4 days. Validates FR-20, FR-21, FR-22, FR-28.
484	- **SM-2:** Paper checklist retirement — percentage of valve-exercise inspections conducted through Tidewatch rather than paper in each pilot city, target 100% by end of the parallel-run period (§9). Validates FR-11, FR-12.
485	
486	**Secondary**
487	- **SM-3:** Cadence compliance — percentage of valves (and other cadence-governed Assets) exercised/tested on schedule, by District, trending upward over the pilot. Validates FR-34, FR-35.
488	- **SM-4:** Sync reliability — percentage of field sync attempts completing within the 90-second target (§6), and overall sync success rate. Validates FR-4, FR-5.
489	- **SM-5:** Evidence completeness — percentage of Findings with all template-required evidence (photo, signature, GPS) captured, directly addressing the "photos get lost" and "GPS typed from memory" problems named in §1. Validates FR-9, FR-10, FR-13, FR-14, FR-15.
490	
491	**Counter-metrics (do not optimize)**
492	- **SM-C1:** Per-inspection time — median time from Asset identification to Finding submission must not increase versus the pre-Tidewatch paper-and-camera baseline. Counterbalances SM-1 and SM-2: a faster-to-work-order, more-complete record that takes inspectors meaningfully longer per stop isn't the win it looks like on paper.
493	- **SM-C2:** Review Queue volume per Crew-day — Exception count should not grow simply because Template tolerances (FR-11) are configured too tightly; a ballooning queue indicates false-positive triage burden on supervisors (R8), not genuine problem detection. Counterbalances SM-1 (escalation speed) and SM-3 (cadence pressure shouldn't push tolerances loose or tight for the wrong reasons).
494	
495	## 15. Open Questions
496	
497	Items marked **[build-blocking]** sit directly under the integration surface and should close before architecture/story-breakdown starts; the rest are pilot-time or go-to-market items that don't block that work.
498	
499	1. **[build-blocking]** Which specific GIS/work-order systems do the two actual pilot cities run (Cityworks, Lucity, ArcGIS Enterprise/Online, Maximo, something else, or nothing at all)? FR-27/FR-28 are specified generically; real integration scoping needs this confirmed per city.
500	2. **[build-blocking]** What is each pilot city's actual regulatory retention requirement for backflow-testing and valve-exercise records? FR-26 defaults to 7 years pending this.
501	3. Which language(s) beyond English, if any, do pilot-city field crews actually need? v1 is assumed to ship English + Spanish for the field app (§6 Localization) — confirm this covers real pilot-crew demographics, or whether additional/different languages are needed.
502	4. How time-sensitive do exception notifications (FR-22) really need to be? If a failed backflow test implies an active cross-connection risk, email/in-app may not be fast enough and SMS/push-to-phone should move into v1 scope.
503	5. What's the typical/maximum contractor engagement length at these utilities? FR-33 defaults to a 90-day cap pending this.
504	6. Is there a target pilot launch date or milestone, or does the timeline stay fully dependent on each city's procurement cycle (§8)?
505	7. What's the intended pricing/packaging model (per-seat, per-asset, flat enterprise license)? Not addressed in this PRD; needed before go-to-market planning.
506	8. **[build-blocking]** Which identity providers do pilot cities actually run (Azure AD, Okta, ADFS, other)? FR-30 assumes standard SAML/OIDC support is sufficient.
507	9. What's the source and licensing model for offline basemap tiles (FR-7), since the utility's own GIS may or may not already provide a cacheable basemap layer?
508	10. How is the equipment/calibration register referenced in FR-25 (torque wrench, flow gauge calibration dates) maintained — inside Tidewatch, or imported from an existing calibration-tracking system?
509	11. Should drone/robotic-crawler input sources (explicitly parked, not rejected) be scoped for a defined v2, or left fully open?
510	
511	## 16. Assumptions Index
512	
513	- §4.1 FR-3 — No v1 template defines a derived/calculated field; the exclusion-from-auto-merge rule is specified defensively for future templates.
514	- §4.1 FR-3 — Attachment (photo/signature) fields use additive-union merge rather than scalar BASE/YOURS/THEIRS comparison; only a single-valued slot edited on both sides produces a Conflict.
515	- §4.1 FR-4 — Delta/field-level sync (not full-record re-upload) is necessary to meet the 90-second/200-record target.
516	- §4.2 FR-7 — Offline map *viewing* (not authoring) is in scope for v1; basemap/Asset layers pre-sync whenever connectivity is available.
517	- §4.2 FR-9 — GPS is captured fix-on-demand at point of use, not via continuous background tracking, to meet the battery NFR.
518	- §4.2 FR-10 — No manual free-text coordinate entry is offered as a fallback to Snap-to-Asset; out-of-tolerance cases keep the raw captured fix.
519	- §4.3 FR-14 — Target photo compression of ~2000-3000px long edge at ~70-85% JPEG quality.
520	- §4.3 FR-16 — Touch-target (9mm/44px) and high-contrast-mode (7:1) numeric bounds are starting targets, not utility-confirmed requirements.
521	- §4.6 FR-25 — Equipment/calibration metadata is entered or selected by the inspector from a utility-maintained equipment register; the register's own maintenance mechanism is unspecified (see Open Question 10).
522	- §4.6 FR-26 — 7-year default retention floor, utility-configurable.
523	- §4.7 FR-27 — Asset-register write-back is analyst-approval-gated, not auto-committed.
524	- §4.8 FR-30 — Standards-based SAML/OIDC SSO is sufficient for v1; no bespoke per-IdP integration assumed.
525	- §4.7 FR-29 — Bounded retry (exponential backoff, retrying over a 24-hour window) before an integration operation moves to a visible "failed" state.
526	- §4.8 FR-32 — Device-bound tokens remain usable offline for up to 7 days without server contact before the device locks out pending reconnection.
527	- §4.8 FR-33 — 90-day default maximum Contractor-account expiration, administrator-configurable.
528	- §4.5 FR-22 — In-app + email notification channels for v1; SMS deferred.
529	- §6 — Reference weak-LTE profile (~1 Mbps down / 512 kbps up, ~150ms latency, ~1% packet loss) for the 90-second sync NFR.
530	- §6 — Battery NFR achievable only with duty-cycled GPS and batched sync, not continuous operation.
531	- §6 — Device OS floors: Android 11+, iOS 16+.
532	- §6 — Localization: field app ships English + Spanish for v1; supervisor/web app is English-only; confirm against pilot-crew demographics (Open Question 3).
533	- §6 — Data residency means the deploying utility's own state/country, configurable per pilot city.
534	- §6 — Security key-management posture: AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2+ in transit, 90-day key-rotation cadence — no utility-specific policy confirmed.
535	- §6 — 99.5% uptime target for the web app/sync backend, excluding scheduled maintenance; not itself an incident-response SLA against SM-1.
536	- §7 — Tidewatch is framed as having no functional-safety requirements since it performs no physical control actuation.
537	- §8 — A union/labor stakeholder is relevant for at least some pilot cities with organized field workforces.

13:This PRD specifies Tidewatch, an offline-first field inspection app for municipal water-main inspectors, for the product manager, pilot-city stakeholders (utility IT/security, GIS/asset management, compliance, field operations), and downstream workflow owners (UX, architecture, epic/story breakdown). It is structured so that Glossary terms (§3) are used verbatim throughout, user journeys (§2.3) are referenced by ID from the functional requirements that realize them (§4), and every `[ASSUMPTION]` made in the absence of confirmed input is both tagged inline and indexed in §9 for explicit sign-off. No prior inputs (brief, research, UX docs) existed for this PRD; it was built from a single founding brain-dump plus targeted web research on comparable products, offline-sync patterns, and the regulatory landscape — all folded in below rather than kept as a separate document.
129:A full day's queued data for one device — up to 200 Findings with attached photos — completes syncing within 90 seconds against the reference weak-LTE profile defined in §6 Cross-Cutting NFRs.
262:Supervisors receive an in-app and email notification when a new Exception enters their Review Queue. `[ASSUMPTION: in-app + email covers v1; SMS/push-to-phone for time-sensitive exceptions (e.g., a failed backflow test) is deferred pending confirmation of how time-sensitive these actually need to be — see §8 Open Questions.]`
289:- Equipment calibration date is present for any Template field that designates calibrated-equipment evidence (e.g., torque wrench, flow gauge). `[ASSUMPTION: equipment/calibration metadata is entered or selected by the inspector at capture time from a utility-maintained equipment register — the mechanism for maintaining that register is not yet specified; see §8 Open Questions.]`
331:Users authenticate via the utility's identity provider using a standard SSO protocol. `[ASSUMPTION: standards-based SAML/OIDC support is sufficient for v1 rather than bespoke per-IdP integrations — specific pilot-city IdPs (Azure AD, Okta, ADFS, etc.) are unconfirmed; see §8 Open Questions.]`
358:**Description:** The view that answers "are we actually keeping up with the valve-exercise program," which today nobody can answer without manually counting paper. Realizes the business goal in §1 Vision directly, rather than a specific UJ.
405:**Cost:** No cost ceiling or pricing model was specified by the product owner; flagged as an Open Question (§8) rather than assumed, since it affects packaging decisions this PRD doesn't own.
411:- **Utility IT/Security** — SSO integration (FR-30), device management policy, data residency (§6).
414:- **Field Operations director** — the likely procurement sponsor; rollout and training plan (§9) sign-off.
426:- **Residency:** In-region per §6.
428:- **Classification:** Operational/Asset data is non-PII by default; field-staff identity is the primary PII category, handled as employment-related data rather than customer data (§7 Privacy).
432:This section documents the regulatory/standards context Tidewatch's audit and reporting features (§4.6) are built to satisfy — grounded in research rather than assumption, since getting this wrong undermines the product's core value proposition:
437:- **Asset-management reporting:** GASB 34's "modified approach" lets utilities skip infrastructure depreciation in financial statements if they maintain a current asset inventory, documented condition assessments via a reproducible method performed at least every 3 years, evidence of a maintained condition level, and estimated annual maintenance cost — plus required supplementary disclosure of actual-versus-estimated preservation spending for each of the past 5 reporting periods. §4.6's audit trail and §4.9's cadence dashboard directly support the condition-assessment and spending-disclosure evidence trail this requires. AWWA G200/G400 series provide the underlying voluntary standards of practice for documentation and record retention.
438:- **Accessibility:** WCAG 2.2 AA for the supervisor/auditor/GIS-analyst web app (§6).
444:- **R1 — GPS inaccuracy, or complete signal loss, underground undermines Snap-to-Asset and location capture.** Mitigated by always displaying accuracy radius (FR-9), providing an explicit "no fix" flag with a manual-reconciliation path when no GPS signal is obtainable at all (FR-9), and falling back to scan/map/nearest-N identification (§4.2) rather than forcing a low-confidence snap.
445:- **R2 — 12-18 month procurement cycles delay pilot start.** Mitigated by engaging IT/Security and Compliance stakeholders (§8) early, in parallel with commercial negotiation rather than sequentially after it.
447:- **R4 — Crew resistance to replacing a familiar paper workflow.** Mitigated by the parallel-run rollout approach (§9) rather than a forced cutover.
449:- **R6 — State-specific regulatory variance** (especially backflow-testing cadence/recordkeeping). Mitigated by configurable Templates (FR-11) and retention policy (FR-26) rather than one hard-coded ruleset; see §11 note.
450:- **R7 — Battery and sync-performance NFR targets prove infeasible under real field conditions.** Mitigated by validating fix-on-capture GPS and batched/delta sync (§6) against real pilot-site network and device conditions early in the pilot, before wider rollout.
451:- **R8 — Exception-based review queue (FR-20) either misses real problems (tolerances too loose) or buries supervisors (tolerances too tight).** Mitigated by making tolerances configurable per Template (FR-11) and tracked directly via the SM-C2 counter-metric (§13).
453:- **R10 — Approval and retry queues (FR-27 GIS write-back, FR-29 integration retries) could grow silently unbounded** (a GIS analyst on leave; a long-dead work-order integration), with field crews re-flagging the same discrepancy on every revisit. Mitigated by write-back proposal deduplication (FR-27), backlog visibility via §6 Observability, and bounded retry with escalation to a visible "failed" state after a maximum attempt count (FR-29).
477:- SMS notifications for exceptions — deferred pending confirmation of how time-sensitive exceptions really need to be (§8 Open Questions).
484:- **SM-2:** Paper checklist retirement — percentage of valve-exercise inspections conducted through Tidewatch rather than paper in each pilot city, target 100% by end of the parallel-run period (§9). Validates FR-11, FR-12.
488:- **SM-4:** Sync reliability — percentage of field sync attempts completing within the 90-second target (§6), and overall sync success rate. Validates FR-4, FR-5.
489:- **SM-5:** Evidence completeness — percentage of Findings with all template-required evidence (photo, signature, GPS) captured, directly addressing the "photos get lost" and "GPS typed from memory" problems named in §1. Validates FR-9, FR-10, FR-13, FR-14, FR-15.

content.content:
1	# Editorial Lenses — Common Ground
2	
3	Shared by the `structure` and `prose` lenses. Load this once; when both lenses run, the setup below is done once and serves both.
4	
5	## Stance
6	
7	Review a document as a clinical editor and return suggested fixes the author can accept or reject row by row. Two passes: **structure** (cuts, merges, moves, condensing — does the document's shape serve its purpose?) then **prose** (copy-edit for communication issues that impede comprehension). Which of the two run, and in what order, is decided by lens selection — see the skill's Execution section.
8	
9	**Content is sacrosanct.** Never challenge ideas — only how they're organized and expressed. Propose, don't execute: the author decides what to accept.
10	
11	The baseline style guide is `{workflow.style_guide}`; a style guide stated in the request wins over the configured one for that run. Where the style guide in effect conflicts with a generic principle here — including the reader calibration — the style guide wins. Nothing overrides content being sacrosanct.
12	
13	## Setup
14	
15	1. Gather inputs: the content (required — a path or pasted text), plus whatever the request states: purpose, target audience, length target, reader type, style guide. If no reviewable content was provided, say so and stop. Request-level values win; `{workflow.reader_type}` and `{workflow.style_guide}` fill what the request leaves unstated. Treat `{workflow.review_guidance}` entries as standing review directives.
16	2. When the content is a file, get exact word counts — document total and per heading section — via `uv run {skill-root}/scripts/word_metrics.py <path>` (`--help` documents the output), and ground every word-impact estimate and the reduction summary in those numbers. If the content was pasted or the script cannot run, estimate and mark the numbers as estimates.
17	3. Infer purpose and audience from the content and standing context when not provided, and open the output with your one-sentence read — "this document exists to help [audience] accomplish [goal]" — so the author can correct a wrong premise before acting on the findings.
18	
19	## Reader calibration
20	
21	Calibrate every finding to the reader type — stated in the request, else `{workflow.reader_type}`.
22	
23	**humans** (default) — optimize for clarity, flow, and natural progression. These elements serve comprehension and engagement; preserve them unless clearly wasteful, and flag any recommendation that would cut one:
24	
25	- Visual aids: diagrams, images, and flowcharts anchor understanding
26	- Expectation-setting: "What You'll Learn" helps readers confirm they're in the right place
27	- Reader's journey: organize content as a linear progression, not a database
28	- Mental models: overview before details prevents cognitive overload
29	- Warmth: encouraging tone reduces anxiety for new users
30	- Whitespace: admonitions and callouts provide visual breathing room
31	- Summaries: recaps help retention; they're reinforcement, not redundancy
32	- Examples: concrete illustrations make abstract concepts accessible
33	- Engagement: flow techniques (transitions, variety) are functional, not fluff — they maintain attention
34	
35	**llm** — optimize for precision and unambiguity. An LLM-targeted document may run longer where explicitness pays and shorter where warmth was cut:
36	
37	- Dependency-first: define concepts before usage to minimize hallucination risk
38	- Cut emotional language, encouragement, and orientation sections
39	- Reference well-known standards ("conventional commits", "REST APIs") instead of re-teaching them; be explicit where a concept is not well-known — and either way, ground the expectation with an example
40	- Consistent terminology: same word for same concept throughout
41	- No hedging ("might", "could", "generally") — direct statements
42	- Prefer structured formats (tables, lists, YAML) over prose
43	- Unambiguous references: no unclear antecedents ("it", "this", "the above")
44	
45	## Findings shape
46	
47	The editorial lenses render as a findings table rather than the canonical JSON fields. One findings table serves both passes:
48	
49	| Pass      | Original Text                                         | Revised Text                                  | Changes                                                              |
50	| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
51	| structure | §Setup — full section (~180 words)                    | MERGE into §Installation                      | Duplicates the install steps; one source of truth (saves ~150 words) |
52	| prose     | The system will processes data and it handles errors. | The system processes data and handles errors. | Fixed subject-verb agreement; removed redundant "it"                 |
53	
54	Structure rows name the section or passage in **Original Text** and carry the tagged disposition (with move target or condensed rewrite) in **Revised Text**; prose rows quote the exact text and its revision. Order rows by comprehension impact; when a long document would produce more rows than an author can realistically act on, present the highest-impact rows and roll the rest into one closing line — "N further minor fixes; ask to expand." Above the table, give the purpose/audience read plus — when the structure pass ran — the chosen structure model. When the structure pass ran, close with a summary: total recommendations, estimated reduction (words and % of original, computed from the word-metrics counts) if all are accepted, whether a provided length target is met, and any comprehension trade-offs (cuts that sacrifice reader engagement for brevity). A pass that finds nothing is a valid result; say so.
55	
56	Shape the table per `{workflow.output_preferences}`.
57

15	## 1. Vision
16	
17	Municipal water utilities run safety- and compliance-critical field programs — exercising every valve on a schedule so it doesn't seize before an emergency, flow-testing hydrants so fire response has the pressure it needs, verifying backflow preventers so contaminated water can't siphon into the drinking supply — on paper checklists and a pocket camera. The paper doesn't argue back: GPS coordinates get typed from memory and are wrong, photos get separated from the finding they were evidence for, and a finding sits in a clipboard for days before it becomes a work order. When a state auditor asks for the trail, someone reconstructs it from scanned PDFs. When a valve-exercise program falls behind cadence, nobody notices until the valve fails during a main break.
18	
19	Tidewatch replaces that paper trail with a field app built for the conditions it will actually be used in — gloved hands, sun glare, concrete vaults with no signal — and a companion web app for the people who schedule the work, review exceptions, and answer to regulators. It captures inspections offline for days at a time, ties every finding to a GPS-verified, auditor's-identity-and-equipment-stamped, photo- and signature-backed record the moment it's created, and syncs it the instant a connection appears — without losing data when two field crews touch the same asset while both were offline. It writes clean corrections back to the utility's GIS asset register instead of letting field reality and the official record drift apart, and it turns four days of paper re-keying into a work order that exists within the same shift the problem was found.
20	
21	For a mid-size utility piloting Tidewatch, success looks like this: the valve-exercising program runs entirely through the app, with nobody keeping a parallel paper trail "just in case," and the 4-day gap between an inspector finding something wrong and a work order existing to fix it collapses to under four hours — without inspectors spending any longer per inspection than they did with a clipboard.
22	
23	## 2. Target User
24	
25	### 2.1 Jobs To Be Done
26	
27	- **Field inspectors** — capture an accurate, defensible finding on the first try, even with no signal and gloves on, without having to re-key or reconcile it later; protect themselves from "did you actually test this" disputes with a timestamped, located, photographed record.
28	- **Dispatchers/supervisors** — know where every crew and every overdue asset stands without waiting for end-of-day paper to land on a desk; spend review time only on findings that are actually anomalous, not re-reading everything that went fine.
29	- **Compliance auditors** — produce a regulator-ready packet for a reporting period without manually reconstructing history from scanned PDFs and whoever remembers what happened.
30	- **GIS analysts** — keep the asset register accurate as field reality changes (a relocated valve, a replaced hydrant) without manual re-entry from field notes, and without untrusted field edits landing directly in the system of record.
31	- **Contractors** (secondary) — get exactly the access needed for a time-boxed engagement, nothing more, without becoming a standing account someone has to remember to deactivate.

34	
35	- Residents/customers receiving outage notifications — no customer-facing surface in v1.
36	- Hydraulic modeling engineers — modeling is out of scope.
37	- Meter-reading/AMI field staff — different workflow, different asset class, out of scope.
38	- Sewer and stormwater field crews — v1 is water mains only.
